name: QASC
fullName: Quality in Acute Stroke Care: implementation of evidence-based treatment protocols to manage fever, hyperglycaemia, and swallowing dysfunction in acute stroke
population: n=1696, adults ≥18 y, NIHSS unselected stroke severity; benefit reported as present irrespective of severity, presentation ≤48 h of symptom onset
finding: POSITIVE: intervention-unit patients were significantly less likely to be dead or dependent — 236/558 (42%) vs 259/449 (58%) — number needed to treat 6.4
teachingPoint: Supports enforcing a nurse-initiated fever/glucose/swallowing protocol on admission as a package rather than leaving each element to individual discretion.

name: CLOTS 3
fullName: Effectiveness of intermittent pneumatic compression in reduction of risk of deep vein thrombosis in patients who have had a stroke (CLOTS 3)
population: n=2876, median 76 y (IQR 67-84), NIHSS not reported; immobility used as the entry criterion instead of NIHSS, enrolled day 0 to day 3 of hospital admission
finding: POSITIVE: proximal DVT in 122/1438 (8.5%) with IPC vs 174/1438 (12.1%) without — absolute risk reduction 3.6%
teachingPoint: Supports applying intermittent pneumatic compression from the day of admission in stroke patients who cannot walk to the toilet unaided, with daily skin inspection.

name: CLOTS 1
fullName: Effectiveness of thigh-length graduated compression stockings to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis after stroke (CLOTS trial 1)
population: n=2518, adults; trial enrolled a broadly representative immobile stroke population, NIHSS not reported; immobility used as the entry criterion, admitted to hospital within 1 week of acute stroke
finding: DID NOT meet its aim — NULL: proximal DVT in 126/1256 (10.0%) with stockings vs 133/1262 (10.5%) without, a non-significant absolute risk reduction of 0.5%
teachingPoint: Argues against ordering thigh-length graduated compression stockings for VTE prophylaxis after stroke, given no measured benefit and a four-fold excess of skin injury.

name: PREVAIL
fullName: The efficacy and safety of enoxaparin versus unfractionated heparin for the prevention of venous thromboembolism after acute ischaemic stroke (PREVAIL Study)
population: n=1762, adults, NIHSS stratified at randomisation: severe stroke NIHSS ≥14 vs less severe NIHSS <14, randomised within 48 h of symptom onset
finding: POSITIVE for the composite: 68/666 (10%) with enoxaparin vs 121/669 (18%) with unfractionated heparin — a 43% relative reduction
teachingPoint: Informs the choice between once-daily enoxaparin and twice-daily unfractionated heparin for VTE prophylaxis in non-ambulatory ischaemic stroke, with extracranial bleeding as the trade-off to weigh.

name: FOOD (Trials 2 and 3)
fullName: Effect of timing and method of enteral tube feeding for dysphagic stroke patients (FOOD): a multicentre randomised controlled trial
population: n=1180, adults admitted with stroke and dysphagia, NIHSS not reported; dysphagia requiring consideration of tube feeding was the entry criterion, Trial 2 enrolled within 7 days of admission; Trial 3 within 30 days of admission
finding: BOTH comparisons DID NOT meet significance on the primary endpoint. Trial 2 (early vs avoid): absolute reduction in death of 5.8% (p=0.09, not significant) but a reduction in death or poor outcome of only 1.2% (p=0.7) — i.e. the primary endpoint was flat, with the direction of effect being fewer deaths and more dependent survivors. Trial 3 (PEG vs nasogastric): absolute INCREASE in risk of death of 1.0% (p=0.9) and an increased risk of death or poor outcome of 7.8% (p=0.05), i.e. borderline evidence of harm from starting with PEG
teachingPoint: Frames tube-feeding decisions after stroke as a survival-versus-dependency trade-off and argues against starting with a PEG rather than a nasogastric tube in newly dysphagic patients.

name: SO2S
fullName: Effect of Routine Low-Dose Oxygen Supplementation on Death and Disability in Adults With Acute Stroke: The Stroke Oxygen Study Randomized Clinical Trial
population: n=8003, mean 72 y (SD 13); 4398 (55%) men, NIHSS median NIHSS 5 — a predominantly mild stroke population, enrolled within 24 h of hospital admission
finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: no benefit of prophylactic oxygen at any dose or schedule. Unadjusted OR for a better outcome 0.97 for oxygen vs control, and 1.03 for continuous vs nocturnal oxygen. No subgroup could be identified that benefited
teachingPoint: Argues against routine prophylactic supplemental oxygen in non-hypoxic stroke patients; treat the measured desaturation, not the diagnosis.

name: HeadPoST
fullName: Head Positioning in Acute Stroke Trial: cluster-randomized, crossover trial of head positioning in acute stroke
population: n=11093, adults with acute stroke, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract; 85% of strokes were ischaemic, position initiated soon after hospital admission; median 14 h from symptom onset (IQR 5-35 h) and maintained for 24 h
finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: no significant shift in the 90-day mRS distribution between lying flat and sitting up
teachingPoint: Removes routine head-of-bed position from the list of things that change stroke outcome, leaving it a patient-specific judgement about perfusion or aspiration risk.

name: PASS
fullName: The Preventive Antibiotics in Stroke Study (PASS): a pragmatic randomised open-label masked endpoint clinical trial
population: n=2550, adults with acute stroke, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract, randomised within 24 h of symptom onset
finding: DID NOT meet — NULL: preventive ceftriaxone did not affect the distribution of 90-day mRS scores
teachingPoint: Argues against prophylactic antibiotics as part of the stroke admission bundle; antibiotics are for documented infection.

name: SHINE
fullName: Stroke Hyperglycemia Insulin Network Effort (SHINE): Intensive vs Standard Treatment of Hyperglycemia and Functional Outcome in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
population: n=1151, mean 66 y (SD 13.1); 529 (46%) women, NIHSS not reported in the primary publication abstract; the primary outcome was adjusted for baseline stroke severity, enrolled within 12 h of stroke onset; treatment for up to 72 h
finding: DID NOT meet — NULL, and enrolment was STOPPED FOR FUTILITY at a prespecified interim analysis: favourable outcome in 119/581 (20.5%) with intensive control vs 123/570 (21.6%) with standard control
teachingPoint: Argues against intensive IV insulin targeting 80-130 mg/dL after ischaemic stroke; a moderate target avoids the hypoglycaemia without giving up any measured functional benefit.

name: AVERT dose-response
fullName: Prespecified dose-response analysis for A Very Early Rehabilitation Trial (AVERT)
population: n=2104, aged ≥18 y, NIHSS baseline stroke severity was a modelled covariate and a top CART splitting variable; range not stated in the abstract, admitted to a stroke unit within 24 h of stroke onset
finding: The two dose dimensions pull in OPPOSITE directions: greater daily frequency of out-of-bed sessions improved the odds of a favourable outcome (OR 1.13), while greater amount of mobilisation in minutes per day REDUCED the odds of a good outcome (OR 0.94), each holding the other and time to first mobilisation constant
teachingPoint: Supports framing early mobilisation orders around short, frequent out-of-bed sessions rather than total minutes, while flagging that the randomised dose question was not settled by this analysis.
